category: Core vocabulary: time and the calendar

entries.meaning: A unit of time equal to one sixtieth of a minute. ---
examples: Give me a second to find my keys.
The whole thing took about thirty seconds.
He beat his old record by two seconds.

entries.meaning: A unit of time equal to sixty seconds. ---
examples: The bus leaves in five minutes.
Do you have a minute to talk?
Wait a minute — that isn't what she said.
entries.contrast: The noun is MIN-it, but the adjective minute (крошечный) is my-NOOT, with the stress on the second syllable.

entries.meaning: Hour has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The flight takes about three hours.
She studies for an hour every evening.
We waited in line for half an hour.
Our hours are nine to five, Monday through Friday.
The library posted its new summer hours.
The professor holds office hours on Tuesdays.

senses.head: A unit of time equal to sixty minutes
examples: The flight takes about three hours.
She studies for an hour every evening.
We waited in line for half an hour.

senses.head: The set times when a place is open or a person is available or at work
examples: Our hours are nine to five, Monday through Friday.
The library posted its new summer hours.
The professor holds office hours on Tuesdays.

entries.contrast: The h is silent, so the word takes an, not a: an hour.

entries.meaning: A period of twenty-four hours, or the light part of it. ---
examples: I'll call you in a couple of days.
What a beautiful day it is.
She works six days a week.

entries.meaning: A period of seven days. ---
examples: We're going to Chicago next week.
The class meets twice a week.
I've been sick for two weeks.
entries.contrast: Week and weak (слабый) are perfect homophones in American English.

entries.meaning: One of the twelve periods that a year is divided into. ---
examples: My lease is up at the end of the month.
The baby is only three months old.
It rained almost every day last month.

entries.meaning: A period of twelve months. ---
examples: She moved to Texas two years ago.
This has been a good year for the company.
He saved all year for the trip.

entries.meaning: A period of ten years. ---
examples: The house hasn't been painted in decades.
She spent a decade teaching high school.
Crime has dropped over the past decade.
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable — DEK-ayd, unlike Russian «декАда». It also means ten years, not ten days.

entries.meaning: A period of one hundred years. ---
examples: The church is more than four centuries old.
Photography changed art in the last century.
This bridge has stood for over a century.

entries.meaning: A period of two weeks. ---
examples: They stayed with us for a fortnight.
The results come back within a fortnight.
He wrote to her every fortnight that summer.
entries.contrast: Mainly British. Americans understand fortnight but almost always say two weeks.

entries.meaning: An extremely long period of time. ---
examples: These rocks formed eons ago.
It feels like an eon since we last talked.
The river took eons to carve the canyon.

entries.meaning: A long stretch of history with a particular character. ---
examples: The telephone opened a new era in communication.
That song belongs to a different era.
Both eras produced great architecture.

entries.meaning: A distinct period in history or in the development of something. ---
examples: The moon landing marked an epoch in space travel.
Geologists divide the past into epochs.
We're living through an epoch of rapid change.
entries.contrast: The ch is said like k, and the word is stressed on the first syllable — EP-uhk, unlike Russian «эпОха».

entries.meaning: Age has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She learned to read at the age of four.
Children under the age of twelve get in free.
It took ages to get through security.
I haven't seen Marcus in ages.
It took ages to get through security.
We waited ages for a table and then gave up.

senses.head: How old someone or something is, or a long period of history
examples: She learned to read at the age of four.
Children under the age of twelve get in free.
It took ages to get through security.

senses.head: A very long time
examples: I haven't seen Marcus in ages.
It took ages to get through security.
We waited ages for a table and then gave up.

entries.русский: возраст; эпоха; целая вечность, очень долго

entries.meaning: Generation has 3 distinct senses.
examples: My grandmother's generation saved everything.
The farm has been in the family for four generations.
This generation grew up with smartphones.
The new generation of electric trucks goes twice as far.
This phone is two generations behind mine.
The camera is in its fourth generation now.
Wind now accounts for a third of the state's power generation.
The plant's generation dropped during the heat wave.
Their whole marketing budget goes to lead generation.

senses.head: All the people born and living at about the same time
examples: My grandmother's generation saved everything.
The farm has been in the family for four generations.
This generation grew up with smartphones.

senses.head: One model or version in a series of products, each replacing the one before it
examples: The new generation of electric trucks goes twice as far.
This phone is two generations behind mine.
The camera is in its fourth generation now.

senses.head: The producing of something such as electricity, heat, or income
examples: Wind now accounts for a third of the state's power generation.
The plant's generation dropped during the heat wave.
Their whole marketing budget goes to lead generation.

entries.русский: поколение; поколение (модели, версии устройства); выработка, производство (энергии, дохода)

entries.meaning: The whole length of a person's life. ---
examples: He saw the country change in his lifetime.
That was the trip of a lifetime.
The pan is supposed to last a lifetime.

entries.meaning: The length of time a person, animal, or thing lives or lasts. ---
examples: A housefly has a very short lifespan.
Average lifespans have risen steadily.
The roof has a lifespan of about thirty years.

entries.meaning: The length of time something continues. ---
examples: Please stay seated for the duration of the flight.
The duration of the course is six weeks.
He said nothing for the whole duration of the meeting.

entries.meaning: A period of time between two events. ---
examples: Take one pill at four-hour intervals.
There was a long interval between the two storms.
Buses run at ten-minute intervals.

entries.meaning: Span has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She wrote four novels in the span of a year.
His attention span is about ten minutes.
The study covers a span of two decades.
The bridge has a span of four hundred feet.
He measured the span of his hand against the board.
Both spans of the bridge were rebuilt.

senses.head: The length of time that something lasts or covers
examples: She wrote four novels in the span of a year.
His attention span is about ten minutes.
The study covers a span of two decades.

senses.head: The distance from one end of something to the other
examples: The bridge has a span of four hundred feet.
He measured the span of his hand against the board.
Both spans of the bridge were rebuilt.

entries.meaning: A very short period of time. ---
examples: Could you wait a moment?
For a moment I thought he was serious.
We had a few quiet moments before the guests arrived.

entries.meaning: An extremely short moment of time. ---
examples: The lights went out in an instant.
For an instant nobody moved.
She knew his voice the instant he spoke.

entries.meaning: A very short time, used mostly in casual speech. ---
examples: I'll be back in a jiffy.
The soup heats up in a jiffy.
He had the tire changed in a jiffy.

entries.meaning: Term has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The senator is serving her second term.
Grades come out at the end of the term.
He signed on for a five-year term.
A senator's term is six years.
He is in his second term as mayor.
Some states limit governors to two terms.

senses.head: A fixed period, such as a school session or a time in office
examples: The senator is serving her second term.
Grades come out at the end of the term.
He signed on for a five-year term.

senses.head: The fixed period a person serves in an elected office
examples: A senator's term is six years.
He is in his second term as mayor.
Some states limit governors to two terms.

entries.meaning: One of the two main periods that an American school year is divided into. ---
examples: I'm taking chemistry next semester.
She studied abroad for a semester.
Both semesters end with final exams.

entries.meaning: One of three periods that a pregnancy or a school year is divided into. ---
examples: She felt tired all through the first trimester.
The baby grows fast in the third trimester.
That school splits the year into three trimesters.

entries.meaning: Session has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We booked an hour-long therapy session.
The legislature is in session until June.
The band recorded three sessions last week.
The bill died at the end of the session.
The governor called a special session.
Two sessions passed with no action on it.

senses.head: A period spent on one activity, or a formal meeting
examples: We booked an hour-long therapy session.
The legislature is in session until June.
The band recorded three sessions last week.

senses.head: A period during which a legislature or court meets and works
examples: The bill died at the end of the session.
The governor called a special session.
Two sessions passed with no action on it.

entries.meaning: Phase has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The project is entering its final phase.
It's just a phase — he'll grow out of it.
The moon goes through eight phases.
Water has three phases: solid, liquid, and gas.
The metal changes phase at that temperature.
We are still in the first phase of the experiment.

senses.head: One stage in a process of change or development
examples: The project is entering its final phase.
It's just a phase — he'll grow out of it.
The moon goes through eight phases.

senses.head: One of the forms that matter can take, or one stage of a process
examples: Water has three phases: solid, liquid, and gas.
The metal changes phase at that temperature.
We are still in the first phase of the experiment.

entries.contrast: Phase and faze (смущать, выбивать из колеи) sound exactly alike.

entries.meaning: Stage has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The illness was caught at an early stage.
We'll do the remodel in three stages.
At this stage nothing has been decided.
The band walked out on stage at nine.
She was nervous the first time she stood on a stage.
The festival has four stages running at once.

senses.head: One step in a longer process
examples: The illness was caught at an early stage.
We'll do the remodel in three stages.
At this stage nothing has been decided.

senses.head: The raised floor where musicians or actors perform
examples: The band walked out on stage at nine.
She was nervous the first time she stood on a stage.
The festival has four stages running at once.

entries.meaning: A series of events that repeat in the same order. ---
examples: The washing machine is running a short cycle.
The news cycle moves fast these days.
These insects have a two-year life cycle.

entries.meaning: The part of the day from sunrise until noon. ---
examples: I drink coffee every morning.
The appointment is Tuesday morning.
Cold mornings make it hard to get up.
entries.contrast: Morning and mourning (траур) are perfect homophones in American English.

entries.meaning: The part of the day between noon and evening. ---
examples: Let's meet Friday afternoon.
She naps most afternoons.
It rained all afternoon.

entries.meaning: The part of the day between the end of the afternoon and bedtime. ---
examples: We usually eat at six in the evening.
He teaches two evenings a week.
It was a warm summer evening.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, not three — EEV-ning. The middle e is not pronounced.

entries.meaning: The dark part of every twenty-four hours. ---
examples: The baby cried all night.
We stayed two nights in Denver.
Drive carefully at night.
entries.contrast: Night and knight (рыцарь) are perfect homophones; the k and the gh are both silent.

entries.meaning: Twelve o'clock at night. ---
examples: The store closes at midnight.
We talked until well past midnight.
The new rules take effect at midnight.

entries.meaning: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day. ---
examples: Checkout is at noon.
By noon the temperature hit ninety.
The parade starts a little before noon.

entries.meaning: The middle part of the day, around twelve o'clock. ---
examples: The heat is worst at midday.
We took a midday break in the shade.
By midday the fog had burned off.

entries.meaning: The time when light first appears in the morning. ---
examples: The crew set out at daybreak.
Birds start singing before daybreak.
We hiked from daybreak until dark.

entries.meaning: The time when the sun goes below the horizon. ---
examples: Be home before sundown.
The temperature drops fast after sundown.
They fish from dawn to sundown.

entries.meaning: The hours between sunrise and sunset. ---
examples: Raccoons rarely come out in the daytime.
Daytime temperatures are staying near freezing.
He works nights and sleeps in the daytime.

entries.meaning: The hours of darkness. ---
examples: Nighttime is when the bakery gets busy.
She's afraid of the nighttime noises outside.
The park is closed at nighttime.

entries.meaning: The day or evening before an important day or event. ---
examples: They arrived on the eve of the wedding.
The team practiced hard on the eve of the big game.
Talks broke down on the eve of the deadline.

entries.meaning: This present day. ---
examples: Today is my last day of work.
Today has been a long one.
The paper never came today.

entries.meaning: Tomorrow has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Tomorrow is supposed to be sunny.
Let's finish this tomorrow.
Tomorrow never seems to come.
These students are the leaders of tomorrow.
The whole exhibit was about the city of tomorrow.
He spends money like there's no tomorrow.

senses.head: The day after today
examples: Tomorrow is supposed to be sunny.
Let's finish this tomorrow.
Tomorrow never seems to come.

senses.head: The future
examples: These students are the leaders of tomorrow.
The whole exhibit was about the city of tomorrow.
He spends money like there's no tomorrow.

entries.meaning: The day before today. ---
examples: Yesterday was busier than usual.
I mailed the check yesterday.
It seems like yesterday that they were kids.

entries.meaning: The night of the present day. ---
examples: Tonight is the season finale.
We're eating out tonight.
Tonight should be clear and cold.

entries.meaning: Saturday and Sunday, when most people don't work. ---
examples: We're driving up for the weekend.
He works most weekends.
Have a good weekend.

entries.meaning: Any day from Monday through Friday. ---
examples: The clinic is open on weekdays only.
Traffic is worse on a weekday.
She swims every weekday morning.

entries.meaning: A day people go to work, or the hours worked in one day. ---
examples: My workday starts at seven.
It was a long workday.
Most workdays end around five.
entries.contrast: Americans write workday; the British usually say working day.

entries.meaning: The days and hours a person works in a week. ---
examples: They moved to a four-day workweek.
A standard workweek is forty hours.
Long workweeks wore him out.
entries.contrast: American; the British say working week.

entries.meaning: Holiday has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bank is closed for the holiday.
Thanksgiving is my favorite holiday.
We get ten paid holidays a year.
We're flying home for the holidays.
The store hires extra help over the holidays.
I gained five pounds during the holidays.

senses.head: A day when most people don't work, usually to mark something
examples: The bank is closed for the holiday.
Thanksgiving is my favorite holiday.
We get ten paid holidays a year.

senses.head: The weeks around Christmas and New Year, usually spoken of as the holidays
examples: We're flying home for the holidays.
The store hires extra help over the holidays.
I gained five pounds during the holidays.

entries.русский: праздник, праздничный день; новогодние и рождественские праздники
entries.contrast: In American English a holiday is a праздник; in British English it also means отпуск, which Americans call a vacation.

entries.meaning: The yearly return of the date on which someone was born. ---
examples: Her birthday is in April.
We threw him a surprise birthday party.
The twins share the same birthday.

entries.meaning: The yearly return of the date of a past event. ---
examples: They celebrated their tenth wedding anniversary.
The town marked the anniversary of the fire.
We never forget those two anniversaries.

entries.meaning: Festival has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The town holds a strawberry festival every June.
We saw three bands at the festival.
Summer festivals draw big crowds.
The town holds a strawberry festival in June.
Both festivals were rained out.
She played at a folk festival in Colorado.

senses.head: A time of public celebration with music, food, or performances
examples: The town holds a strawberry festival every June.
We saw three bands at the festival.
Summer festivals draw big crowds.

senses.head: A public celebration or series of events, often held every year
examples: The town holds a strawberry festival in June.
Both festivals were rained out.
She played at a folk festival in Colorado.

entries.meaning: A large special meal, or a religious day of celebration. ---
examples: Grandma put together a real feast.
The village holds a feast after the harvest.
Their calendar is full of feasts and fasts.

entries.meaning: A special anniversary, usually of twenty-five or fifty years. ---
examples: The college is planning its jubilee.
A parade marked the queen's jubilee.
Both jubilees drew thousands of visitors.
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable — JOO-buh-lee, unlike Russian «юбилЕй».

entries.meaning: An important point or achievement along a longer path. ---
examples: Her first solo flight was a real milestone.
The baby has hit all the usual milestones.
Turning fifty felt like a milestone.

entries.meaning: Timeline has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Here's the timeline for the renovation.
The timeline lists every event of that year.
Both timelines end with the same deadline.
It's still on my timeline from last June.
She cleaned up her timeline before the job interview.
Their timelines are full of vacation photos.

senses.head: A plan or diagram showing when things happen, in order
examples: Here's the timeline for the renovation.
The timeline lists every event of that year.
Both timelines end with the same deadline.

senses.head: The list of a person's posts shown in the order they were made
examples: It's still on my timeline from last June.
She cleaned up her timeline before the job interview.
Their timelines are full of vacation photos.

entries.русский: хронология; график по срокам; лента публикаций, хроника

entries.meaning: The order in which events happened, or a record of that order. ---
examples: The report includes a chronology of the accident.
Nobody could agree on the chronology of that night.
The book ends with a detailed chronology.
entries.contrast: The ch is said like k, and the stress falls on the second syllable — kruh-NAH-luh-jee.

entries.meaning: A book in which someone writes down what happens each day. ---
examples: She kept a diary all through high school.
His war diary was published years later.
Old diaries fill the bottom drawer.
entries.contrast: For Americans a diary is a дневник; the British also use the word for ежедневник, which Americans call a planner.

entries.meaning: Planner has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She writes every assignment in her planner.
I bought a new planner for the school year.
Paper planners are popular again.
City planners want to widen the sidewalk.
We hired a wedding planner to handle the details.
A financial planner walked us through our retirement options.

senses.head: A book or app for writing down appointments and tasks by date
examples: She writes every assignment in her planner.
I bought a new planner for the school year.
Paper planners are popular again.

senses.head: Someone whose job is to plan something such as a city, a wedding, or a budget
examples: City planners want to widen the sidewalk.
We hired a wedding planner to handle the details.
A financial planner walked us through our retirement options.

entries.meaning: A list showing when things are supposed to happen. ---
examples: The train timetable changed in the spring.
We're behind on our timetable.
Both timetables were posted online.

entries.meaning: Something that makes you remember to do something. ---
examples: Set a reminder on your phone.
The dentist sent a reminder about my appointment.
Sticky notes work better for me than digital reminders.

entries.meaning: A count backward to the moment something starts. ---
examples: The countdown to launch began at noon.
Everyone joined the countdown to midnight.
The app runs countdowns for each exam.

entries.meaning: The point at which something stops being valid. ---
examples: Check the expiration date on the milk.
The card is close to expiration.
Expiration of the lease is in June.
entries.contrast: Americans say expiration date; the British say expiry date.

entries.meaning: A year with an extra day in February, coming once every four years. ---
examples: This is a leap year, so February has twenty-nine days.
She was born on the last day of a leap year.
Leap years keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

entries.meaning: A region in which all the clocks are set to the same time. ---
examples: The country spans four time zones.
I keep forgetting the time zone difference.
Set your phone to the local time zone.

entries.meaning: The day of the week after Sunday, when the workweek usually starts. ---
examples: The report is due Monday morning.
Nobody around here likes Mondays.
We start the new schedule on Monday.

entries.meaning: The day of the week between Tuesday and Thursday. ---
examples: Trash pickup is on Wednesday.
She has piano lessons every Wednesday.
Two Wednesdays a month the office closes early.
entries.contrast: Spelled Wed-nes-day but said WENZ-day; the first d and the middle e are silent.

entries.meaning: The day of the week between Wednesday and Friday. ---
examples: The show airs on Thursday nights.
We meet the first Thursday of every month.
Thursdays are always busy at the shop.

entries.meaning: The day of the week between Thursday and Saturday. ---
examples: The office closes early on Friday.
Payday is every other Friday.
Fridays in summer are casual around here.

entries.meaning: The day of the week between Friday and Sunday. ---
examples: We do laundry on Saturday.
The farmers market runs every Saturday.
He works most Saturdays.

entries.meaning: The day of the week between Saturday and Monday. ---
examples: Dinner at my parents' is a Sunday tradition.
The paper is thickest on Sunday.
Sundays always feel too short.

entries.meaning: The second month of the year, with twenty-eight or twenty-nine days. ---
examples: February is the coldest month here.
Her birthday falls in early February.
The last two Februaries were unusually mild.
entries.contrast: Most Americans drop the first r — FEB-yoo-air-ee, not FEB-roo-air-ee.

entries.meaning: March has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The snow usually melts by March.
We're moving at the end of March.
Spring break falls in March this year.
Thousands joined the march on Saturday morning.
There have been three marches downtown this month.
The march ended with speeches on the capitol steps.
The band played a march down Main Street.
That march gets played at every graduation.
Sousa wrote over a hundred marches.

senses.head: The third month of the year
examples: The snow usually melts by March.
We're moving at the end of March.
Spring break falls in March this year.

senses.head: An organized walk by a large group of people to show support for something
examples: Thousands joined the march on Saturday morning.
There have been three marches downtown this month.
The march ended with speeches on the capitol steps.

senses.head: A piece of music with a strong steady beat, written for marching
examples: The band played a march down Main Street.
That march gets played at every graduation.
Sousa wrote over a hundred marches.

entries.meaning: The fourth month of the year. ---
examples: Taxes are due in April.
April here means rain and mud.
The wedding is set for late April.

entries.meaning: The fifth month of the year. ---
examples: Graduation is the third week of May.
The garden looks best in May.
We planted the tomatoes in early May.

entries.meaning: The sixth month of the year. ---
examples: School lets out in June.
Most weddings around here are in June.
June was hotter than usual this year.

entries.meaning: The seventh month of the year. ---
examples: We go to the lake every July.
July is the busiest month for the shop.
The fireworks are on the fourth of July.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable — juu-LY, unlike Russian «Июль».

entries.meaning: The eighth month of the year. ---
examples: August is unbearably humid here.
The store has a big sale every August.
School starts in late August.
entries.contrast: The month is AW-guhst; the rare adjective august (величественный) is aw-GUST.

entries.meaning: The ninth month of the year. ---
examples: Classes start the first week of September.
September is my favorite month.
The leaves begin to turn in late September.

entries.meaning: The tenth month of the year. ---
examples: The apples are ripe in October.
We turn the heat on in October.
Two Octobers ago we had snow before Halloween.

entries.meaning: The eleventh month of the year. ---
examples: Elections are held in November.
November is gray and rainy here.
The lodge opens for the season in November.

entries.meaning: The twelfth and last month of the year. ---
examples: December is our busiest month.
The days are shortest in late December.
We fly home every December.

entries.meaning: Alarm has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My alarm goes off at six.
The fire alarm went off during class.
He sets three alarms every night.
There is no cause for alarm.
She looked up in alarm at the sound.
The numbers caused real alarm at headquarters.

senses.head: A device or sound that wakes you up or warns you
examples: My alarm goes off at six.
The fire alarm went off during class.
He sets three alarms every night.

senses.head: Worry and fear that something is wrong
examples: There is no cause for alarm.
She looked up in alarm at the sound.
The numbers caused real alarm at headquarters.

entries.meaning: Stopwatch has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The coach timed each lap with a stopwatch.
My phone has a stopwatch built in.
The two stopwatches showed different times.
The coach clicked the stopwatch at the finish line.
Time each lap with a stopwatch.
Both stopwatches showed the same split.

senses.head: A watch used to measure exactly how long something takes
examples: The coach timed each lap with a stopwatch.
My phone has a stopwatch built in.
The two stopwatches showed different times.

senses.head: A watch that can be started and stopped to time an event exactly
examples: The coach clicked the stopwatch at the finish line.
Time each lap with a stopwatch.
Both stopwatches showed the same split.

entries.meaning: A glass timer in which sand runs from the top half into the bottom. ---
examples: The board game came with a small hourglass.
The sand ran out of the hourglass in three minutes.
The shop sells antique hourglasses.
entries.contrast: The h is silent, as in hour — OW-ur-glas.

entries.meaning: A device that shows the time by the shadow the sun casts. ---
examples: There's a stone sundial in the garden.
A sundial is useless on a cloudy day.
Old gardens often have sundials.

entries.meaning: A hanging weight that swings back and forth, often to keep a clock running. ---
examples: The pendulum in the hall clock stopped.
He watched the pendulum swing for a while.
Grandfather clocks use heavy pendulums.

entries.meaning: Dial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The watch has a plain black dial.
Turn the dial to set the oven.
The old radio had two dials on the front.
The dial on the oven goes up to 500.
Turn the dial one notch to the right.
The old radio had two dials.

senses.head: The marked face of a clock or a round control you turn
examples: The watch has a plain black dial.
Turn the dial to set the oven.
The old radio had two dials on the front.

senses.head: A round face with numbers on it that shows a reading or sets a level
examples: The dial on the oven goes up to 500.
Turn the dial one notch to the right.
The old radio had two dials.

entries.русский: циферблат; круглый регулятор; циферблат, шкала; регулятор

entries.meaning: Chime has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The clock struck the hour with a soft chime.
We could hear the chimes of the church bells.
Their doorbell has an old-fashioned chime.
Wind chimes clinked on the porch all night.
She hung a brass chime beside the door.
The shop sells chimes made from old silverware.

senses.head: A ringing sound made by a clock or a set of bells
examples: The clock struck the hour with a soft chime.
We could hear the chimes of the church bells.
Their doorbell has an old-fashioned chime.

senses.head: A hanging set of tubes or bells that ring when they move or are struck
examples: Wind chimes clinked on the porch all night.
She hung a brass chime beside the door.
The shop sells chimes made from old silverware.

entries.русский: бой часов, перезвон; музыка ветра; набор колокольчиков

entries.meaning: A short light sleep, or the alarm button that delays waking up. ---
